name: Henderson, TN
spotsNotice: All coordinates are APPROXIMATE. Several spots are 35-55 minutes from Henderson. Verify access, park hours, permits and posted rules before visiting. Fishing in Tennessee requires a TWRA license for anglers 13 and older.

regulations.summary: Anglers 13 and older need a Tennessee fishing license. Size limits, daily creel limits and seasons differ by species and by water body, and they change, so read the current TWRA Fishing Guide every year. State park lakes and Family Fishing Lakes may post their own limits, and the Beech River Watershed lakes need a separate BRWDA permit.

links.label: Buy a license: Go Outdoors Tennessee

tips: Keep your license on you (the Go Outdoors TN app can store it on your phone).
Tennessee usually holds a Free Fishing Day in early June when no license is needed. Check TWRA for the date.
Pickwick Lake borders Alabama and Mississippi. Check TWRA for the current reciprocal license rules before fishing across the state line.

license.trout: Check whether you need TWRA's trout add-on to fish for or keep trout

advisories.summary: Few of the waters around Henderson are on TDEC's main posted list, but the list changes and covers mercury and PCBs in some reservoirs. Check the current TDEC list before you keep fish to eat, especially big catfish and bass from the Tennessee River.

items.title: Large reservoirs and rivers
items.detail: TDEC posts precautionary advisories for mercury or PCBs on some Tennessee reservoirs. Children, pregnant or nursing women, and women who may become pregnant should follow the strictest guidance and eat fewer large, older fish.

items.title: After heavy rain
items.detail: Runoff from farms and roads raises bacteria levels for a day or two in creeks and rivers like the Forked Deer and Hatchie. Wash hands and gear, and cover cuts.

bankSafety: Don't wade the Hatchie or Forked Deer: muddy water hides sudden drop-offs and logs, and the banks are soft.
Below Pickwick Dam, water rises fast when generators start. Horns or sirens mean move to high ground.
West Tennessee bottomlands have ticks, chiggers and snakes in summer. Wear boots and long pants and check for ticks after.

spots.name: Chickasaw State Park: Lake Placid
spots.description: The main lake at Chickasaw State Park, about 15 minutes southwest of Henderson on TN-100. Calm water, easy bank and a boathouse that rents fishing boats and paddleboats (no private boats). The closest and most beginner-friendly spot.
spots.beginnerTip: Fish a worm under a float near the fishing pier or any shady bank. Length and creel limits are posted at the lake, so read the sign first.

spots.name: South Fork Forked Deer River (near Pinson Mounds)
spots.description: The South Fork Forked Deer starts in Chester County and winds north past Pinson Mounds State Archaeological Park toward Jackson. Small, muddy, slow river with lots of fallen timber. Much of the bank is private: only fish where access is clearly public, and ask park staff before fishing on park land.
spots.beginnerTip: Laydowns (fallen trees) hold catfish and sunfish. Drop a nightcrawler on a sinker right beside the log and keep your line tight.

spots.name: Big Hill Pond State Park: Travis McNatt Lake
spots.description: Spring-fed lake in a big wooded state park near Pocahontas, about 35 minutes south. Quiet, with a boat ramp and bank along the dam and day-use area. Electric motors only on the lake.
spots.beginnerTip: Clear, quiet water: use light line and natural colors. A green pumpkin Senko along the weed edges is a good first bass bait.

spots.name: Hatchie River at Bolivar
spots.description: The Hatchie is the last big unchanneled river in the lower Mississippi valley: a muddy, winding, swampy State Scenic River about 35 minutes west. Known for catfish and crappie in the oxbows. Floods spread far into the woods; banks are soft and steep.
spots.beginnerTip: Fish the slack water on the inside of a bend or behind a log jam. Soak cut bait or a nightcrawler on the bottom in the evening.

spots.name: Pickwick Dam tailwater
spots.description: TVA tailwater below Pickwick Dam on the Tennessee River, about 55 minutes southeast near Counce. One of the best tailwaters in the South for smallmouth, sauger and big catfish, with bank fishing and a campground below the dam. Current is strong and rises fast when turbines run.
spots.beginnerTip: Stay behind the railings and out of restricted zones. Sirens or horns mean water releases. Watch what the regulars use and copy them: it is a great place to learn.
spots.advisory: Pickwick Lake is shared with Alabama and Mississippi: check current TWRA reciprocal license rules before fishing above the dam.

spots.name: Tennessee River at Saltillo
spots.description: River town on the upper end of Kentucky Lake, about 50 minutes east, where a small free ferry crosses the Tennessee River. Public ramp area with some bank. Wide water, current and barge traffic.
spots.beginnerTip: Use enough sinker weight to hold bottom in the current. Rocky banks and the mouths of creeks are the best places to start.

spots.name: Beech Lake (Lexington)
spots.description: One of the Beech River Watershed (BRWDA) lakes right beside Lexington, about 35 minutes northeast. The BRWDA lakes need a small daily or annual permit (check current fees with the BRWDA office in Lexington).
spots.beginnerTip: Docks and brush piles hold crappie in spring. Try a Trout Magnet or small minnow under a float right next to the cover.

spots.name: Pine Lake (Beech River Watershed)
spots.description: BRWDA lake southeast of Lexington, lined with docks, points and ledges. Often named by locals as the best fishing of the Lexington lakes. Permit required, like the other BRWDA lakes.
spots.beginnerTip: Fish the points (where the bank sticks out into the lake). Fish move along them between deep and shallow water.

spots.name: Natchez Trace State Park: Brown's Creek Lake
spots.description: 167-acre TWRA Family Fishing Lake in Natchez Trace State Park, about 50 minutes northeast (I-40 exit 116, then TN-114 south). Managed with families and beginners in mind.
spots.beginnerTip: Family Fishing Lakes have their own rules (and sometimes a daily permit): read the sign at the lake. Bluegill on a worm under a float is the easy win here.

spots.name: Natchez Trace State Park: Pin Oak Lake
spots.description: The park's biggest lake (about 690 acres), beside Pin Oak Lodge. Lots of standing timber and shallow coves; famous locally for crappie in spring.
spots.beginnerTip: In March and April crappie move into shallow brush. Fish a small minnow under a float slowly along the timber.

spotsCredit: Suggested spots, descriptions and tips were written by Claude (an AI assistant made by Anthropic) from general knowledge and public listings. Coordinates were not checked against a map and may be off: verify access and rules locally.
